title: Economist breaks down new inflation report and what's driving prices higher
summary: A new report shows US consumer prices rising faster than expected, about 3.7% over the past year, just weeks before the midterm elections. Economist Heather Long explains that energy accounts for only around half of the jump, with medical care, clothing, software and car repairs also getting more expensive, so the Federal Reserve may have to raise rates again. Short interviews with a disabled veteran and a California farmer show how the squeeze feels, and Long describes middle-income families starting to cut back on groceries.
focus: Shadow Heather Long's first answer on why this inflation is broad-based, and her closing answer on how households are coping: crisp economist English with useful phrasing for client updates.

vocab.context: Higher fuel costs are feeding into airfares and heating bills.

vocab.meaning: A specific problem or source of frustration.
vocab.context: Mortgage rates are named as a particular source of strain for households.
vocab.example: Onboarding time is the biggest pain point in the client survey.

vocab.example: We expect freight costs to ease in the second half.

vocab.meaning: Lukewarm; showing little enthusiasm or strength.

vocab.meaning: Continue in a tiring way that slowly wears someone down.

vocab.meaning: Reduce spending or activity, usually out of caution.
vocab.context: Middle-income families are starting to cut back on grocery spending.

vocab.context: Some households are leaning on credit cards for basic needs.

vocab.context: People living on benefits are hit hardest when prices climb.
vocab.example: Retirees on a fixed income are the most price-sensitive segment in our data.

vocab.example: The new feature gave us a small bump in conversion.

vocab.meaning: Pressure that stretches resources or people to their limit.
vocab.context: Long says the financial pressure on households is real.
vocab.example: The hiring freeze is putting a lot of strain on the delivery team.

vocab.meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties.
vocab.context: Describes how middle-class spending had held up until now.
vocab.example: Demand has been surprisingly resilient despite the price increase.

vocab.meaning: Basic things people need, such as food and fuel.
vocab.context: Everyday basics are where households feel price rises most.
vocab.example: In a downturn, shoppers trade down on essentials before cutting them.
